items.answer: Contextual inquiry (CI) is a usability requirement-gathering method, often described as a semi-structured interview process, that observes users performing tasks in their natural work setting and asks users questions to clarify behavior.

questions.question: What does contextual inquiry primarily involve?
options: Observing targeted users in their natural work setting
Testing targeted users in a controlled work setting
Observing targeted users in a controlled work setting
Interviewing targeted users in their natural work setting
questions.explanation: Contextual inquiry is a requirement-gathering method based on observing users in their natural work setting. Interviewing, controlled settings, and testing are not the defining activity of contextual inquiry.

questions.question: What is true of the active mode of contextual inquiry?
options: An observer is absent while the users work
An observer tests users while the users work
An observer advises users while the users work
An observer is present while the users work
questions.explanation: In active mode, the observer is physically present while users do their tasks. The observer is not absent, and advising or testing users is not what defines the active mode.

questions.question: Why should an observer in contextual inquiry act as an apprentice?
options: To assess how quickly users work rather than to advise them
To learn how users behave rather than to advise them
To teach how tasks should be done rather than to advise them
To direct how tasks should be done rather than to advise them
questions.explanation: The observer acts as an apprentice by learning from the users, who are treated as masters. Advising, teaching, directing, or merely assessing performance does not match the apprentice role.

data.text: Contextual inquiry gathers usability requirements by observing users in their natural work setting. It can be carried out actively with an observer present, or passively by reviewing recorded user activities and clarifying issues with users. In either case, the observer should remain an apprentice, learning from users as teachers rather than advising how they should behave.
points: Contextual inquiry gathers usability requirements by observing specified user groups in their natural work setting.
Active contextual inquiry has an observer present, while passive reviews recorded user activities and clarifies issues with users.
The contextual inquiry observer must act as an apprentice, treating users as teachers and not giving advice.

questions.question: In the initiate stage of contextual inquiry, why are end users contacted before workplace observation?
options: To obtain permissions from the relevant authorities so they behave naturally
To remove anxieties that observation may lead to bad outcomes so they behave naturally
To ask them to follow the planned observation script so they behave naturally
To explain the design goals of the inquiry so they behave naturally
questions.explanation: The initiate stage opens communication with end users to reduce worries that the observation may harm them, helping them behave naturally. Contacting users is not primarily for permissions, design goals, or making them follow a script.

questions.question: What is a helpful practice in the plan stage of contextual inquiry?
options: Sending gratitude messages to the users
Obtaining the necessary workplace permissions
Scripting and rehearsing the observation procedure
Sorting the collected observation data into patterns
questions.explanation: The plan stage includes scripting and rehearsing the observation procedure as a helpful practice. Permissions, thank-you messages, and sorting collected data belong to other stages.

questions.question: What is the purpose of using an affinity diagram in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry?
options: To send thank-you notes to users and possibly the authorities after the inquiry
To arrange the collected data so patterns can be found more easily
To identify the users and the date, time, and place of the observation
To obtain all necessary permissions from the relevant authorities before observing
questions.explanation: The affinity diagram method arranges collected data so that patterns become easier to find, supporting the design specification of design goals. It is not used to plan users, obtain permissions, or close the inquiry with thanks.

data.text: Contextual inquiry is carried out through five ordered stages that make usability observation systematic. Planning and initiating prepare the observation, then executing records it and closing finishes it politely. Reflection then organizes the collected data with affinity diagrams, revealing patterns that lead to design goals.
points: The five stages of contextual inquiry systematically run in this order: plan, initiate, execute, close, reflect.
The plan stage sets goals, gathers domain knowledge, and arranges recording, users, time, place, and rehearsal.
The initiate stage obtains permissions and reduces user anxiety so users behave naturally.
The execute stage records observations, and the close stage ideally thanks users and authorities for possible future testing.
The reflect stage uses affinity diagrams to arrange execute-stage data, find patterns, and specify design goals.

activities.title: Order the stages of contextual inquiry

items.title: Order the stages of contextual inquiry
steps: Identify the goals, domain knowledge, users, and observation arrangements
Obtain permissions and ease user anxieties about being observed
Observe users performing their tasks and record what they do
Send thank-you notes to the users and the relevant authorities
Analyze the observation data and identify the design goals

questions.question: In the affinity diagram method, which step is done to find patterns among notes that may look random?
options: Sorting ideas into groups
Drawing the finished diagram
Displaying the raw notes
Naming each sorted group
questions.explanation: Sorting ideas into groups is used to find patterns among notes that may look random. Displaying, naming, and drawing are separate steps.

questions.question: What makes a group header in an affinity diagram different from an original contextual inquiry note?
options: It names the pattern that binds the notes in that group
It states the implementation path chosen for that group
It copies the most detailed original note from that group
It records the observer who collected the data for that group
questions.explanation: A header is created after sorting to label the pattern shared by the grouped notes. It is not a copied note, an observer record, or an implementation instruction.

questions.question: What makes a set of design guidelines informed?
options: They come from recording the users during inquiry
They come from checking the coded implementation
They come from copying a standard app layout
They come from analyzing the collected inquiry data
questions.explanation: Guidelines are informed when they are produced by analyzing collected inquiry data. Recording users, checking code, or copying layouts does not by itself make them informed.

questions.question: In the note-taking example, what does the erase-content recommendation specify?
options: The usability requirement for that feature
The interface placement for that feature
The implementation code for that feature
The user testing plan for that feature
questions.explanation: A design recommendation states the usability requirement without prescribing how it is implemented, who tests it, or where it appears.

data.text: The affinity diagram method organizes contextual inquiry notes by generating, displaying, sorting, and naming them, then drawing the resulting groups. Reflection on the finished diagram turns those grouped patterns into design recommendations. These recommendations are informed by inquiry data, unlike uninformed guidelines made without it, and they state what must be done for usability rather than how to implement it.
points: The affinity diagram method generates and displays contextual inquiry notes, then sorts, names, and diagrams the groups.
Sorting similar notes into groups and adding a header names a pattern not present in the initial ideas.
Reflection on the finished diagram yields design recommendations, informed by inquiry data, unlike uninformed design choices made without it.
A design recommendation is a requirement for usability, not a prescription for implementation.

questions.question: In the calendar affinity diagram, which header contains the observations about checking the day and date in connection with an assignment submission?
options: the day-wise scheduling header
the reminder setting header
the work scheduling header
the overall scheduling header
questions.explanation: The calendar affinity diagram places reminder-related observations, including checking a mobile app date before an assignment submission, under reminder setting. The scheduling headers cover deadline, timetable, meeting, and lecture checking rather than reminders.

questions.question: How did the first non-reminder group in the calendar affinity diagram change before the finished diagram was drawn?
options: overall scheduling became work scheduling and day-wise scheduling
work scheduling became overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling
reminder setting became work scheduling and day-wise scheduling
day-wise scheduling became work scheduling and reminder setting
questions.explanation: The observations about deadlines, timetables, meeting dates, meeting schedules, and lecture schedules were first grouped as work scheduling and then refined into the final overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling groups. The other options reverse the direction of that refinement or place reminder setting in the wrong position.

questions.question: What does the affinity diagram method show about grouping contextual inquiry observations?
options: the users' original written words can be fixed into one final grouping
the recorded order of the observations can be fixed into one final grouping
the observations can be arranged into more than one final grouping
the first chosen headers can be fixed into one final grouping
questions.explanation: An affinity diagram does not force one unique grouping; the same observations can be arranged into different final groups. The recorded order, the users' original words, or the first chosen headers do not determine the grouping.

data.text: Calendar app observations are organized in an affinity diagram to produce requirement categories. Reminder-related observations form the reminder-setting category, while the remaining scheduling observations are first grouped as work scheduling and then refined into overall and day-wise scheduling. This leaves a finished diagram with reminder setting, overall scheduling, and day-wise scheduling. An affinity diagram has no unique grouping, so different groupings are possible.
points: In the calendar app affinity diagram, reminder-related observations are grouped under the reminder-setting header.
The remaining scheduling observations were first grouped as work scheduling, then refined into overall and day-wise scheduling, leaving three groups.
An affinity diagram has no single correct grouping, so different groupings are possible.

Generate ideas
Create a header
Draw finished diagram
items.reason: Generate ideas, create a header, and draw finished diagram are steps of the affinity diagram method, while obtaining permissions is part of the initiate stage of contextual inquiry.

questions.question: Why is the observer's role in genuine contextual inquiry described by the master-apprentice model?
questions.reference_answer: In genuine contextual inquiry, the observer acts as an apprentice or learner while users are masters or teachers. This role requires learning how users behave instead of advising or teaching them, and advice is prohibited. It supports the objective of watching users perform tasks in their natural work setting to gather insight about behavior and requirements.

questions.question: How does affinity diagram analysis connect contextual inquiry observations to design recommendations?
questions.reference_answer: The execute stage of contextual inquiry performs observations and records data. In the reflect stage, the team analyzes that data and identifies design goals, using affinity diagram analysis to arrange the notes so patterns can be found. The finished affinity diagram leads to a design specification, and reflection then formulates design recommendations from the data.

questions.question: Why are design guidelines formulated after an affinity diagram considered informed design choices, while guidelines created without contextual inquiry are not?
questions.reference_answer: Design guidelines are formulated after the finished affinity diagram, so they reflect analysis of collected inquiry data. Guidelines derived from contextual inquiry are informed design choices because they are produced by analyzing that data, ensuring users' needs and expectations are taken into account. Guidelines created without contextual inquiry are uninformed design choices because they do not ensure that users' needs and expectations are taken into account.

questions.question: How does the calendar app affinity diagram example show that there is no unique way to group contextual inquiry observations?
questions.reference_answer: In the calendar app example, five observations not related to reminder setting were first grouped under the header work scheduling. These were then refined into the headers overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling, producing a finished diagram with reminder setting, overall scheduling, and day-wise scheduling. This illustrates that different groupings are possible, because an affinity diagram has no unique way to group observations.
